title: Limits & Continuity
description: What happens as we approach a value?

concepts.title: What is a Limit?
concepts.contentHtml:
A limit describes what value a function approaches as its input gets closer and closer to some number.

Think of it like walking toward a door -- the limit is what's on the other side, even if you never actually step through.

We write it as:

concepts.title: Left and Right Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
Sometimes a function approaches different values depending on which direction you come from.

The left-hand limit is what happens as you approach from below (from the left on the number line). The right-hand limit is from above.

A limit only exists if both sides agree!

concepts.title: Continuity
concepts.contentHtml:
A function is continuous at a point if you can draw it without lifting your pen.

More precisely, f(x) is continuous at x = a when three things are true:

1. f(a) exists (the function is defined there)
2. The limit as x approaches a exists
3. The limit equals f(a)

If any of these fail, we have a discontinuity -- a break, hole, or jump in the graph.

concepts.title: Slope of the Tangent Line
concepts.contentHtml:
The derivative measures how fast a function is changing at any point.

Imagine zooming in on a curve until it looks like a straight line. The slope of that line is the derivative.

We find it by taking two points on the curve, drawing a line between them (a secant line), then sliding the points closer and closer together.

concepts.title: The Power Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
The most useful derivative rule: for any power of x, bring the exponent down as a multiplier and reduce the power by one.

Examples:

x³ becomes 3x²
x⁵ becomes 5x⁴
x¹ becomes 1 (which is just 1)
x² becomes 2x

This simple pattern handles a huge number of functions!

concepts.title: Derivative as a Function
concepts.contentHtml:
The derivative itself is a new function -- it tells you the slope at every point.

If f(x) = x², then f'(x) = 2x. This means:

At x = 1, the slope is 2
At x = 3, the slope is 6
At x = -2, the slope is -4

Where the derivative is positive, the original function is increasing. Where it's negative, the function is decreasing. Where it's zero, we might have a peak or valley.

concepts.title: Area Under a Curve
concepts.contentHtml:
How do you find the area of a shape with curved edges? You can't just use length × width.

The key idea: fill the area with rectangles. The more rectangles you use, the better the approximation. These are called Riemann sums.

As the number of rectangles approaches infinity, the sum approaches the exact area. This is the integral.

concepts.title: Definite vs Indefinite Integrals
concepts.contentHtml:
A definite integral has bounds (from a to b) and gives you a number -- the area.

An indefinite integral has no bounds and gives you a function -- the antiderivative. It answers: "What function has this as its derivative?"

Don't forget the + C! Since the derivative of any constant is zero, there are infinitely many antiderivatives.

concepts.title: The Fundamental Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is one of the most beautiful results in mathematics. It says:

Differentiation and integration are opposites.

If you integrate a function then differentiate the result, you get back to where you started. This connects the two main ideas of calculus into one unified theory.

concepts.title: Optimization
concepts.contentHtml:
One of the most practical uses of calculus: finding the maximum or minimum of a quantity.

The recipe:
1. Write the quantity to optimize as a function
2. Take its derivative
3. Set the derivative equal to zero and solve
4. Check which solutions are maxima vs minima

This works because at a peak or valley, the slope is flat (zero).

concepts.title: Related Rates
concepts.contentHtml:
When two quantities are related and both changing over time, calculus lets us connect their rates of change.

Classic example: a balloon inflating. The radius is growing at some rate. How fast is the volume growing?

Since V = (4/3)πr³, we differentiate both sides with respect to time and substitute the known rate.

concepts.title: Why Calculus Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
Calculus is the language of change, and change is everywhere:

Physics: velocity, acceleration, forces
Biology: population growth, spread of disease
Economics: marginal cost, optimization of profit
Engineering: signal processing, structural analysis
Machine Learning: gradient descent (training neural networks!)

Every time something changes smoothly, calculus is the tool to analyze it.

title: Chain Rule & Product Rule
description: Derivatives of composed and multiplied functions

concepts.title: The Product Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
When two functions are multiplied together, the derivative isn't just the product of their derivatives. Instead:

"First times derivative of second, plus second times derivative of first."

Example: d/dx [x² · sin(x)] = x² cos(x) + 2x sin(x)

Intuitively: both factors are changing simultaneously, and each contributes to the total rate of change.

concepts.title: The Chain Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
The chain rule handles nested functions — a function inside another function.

Think of it as peeling an onion: differentiate the outer layer, then multiply by the derivative of the inner layer.

Example: d/dx [sin(x²)] = cos(x²) · 2x

This is arguably the most important derivative rule. It appears everywhere in multivariable calculus and machine learning (backpropagation is repeated application of the chain rule!).

concepts.title: The Quotient Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
For a fraction of two functions, the quotient rule gives:

"Low d-high minus high d-low, all over the square of what's below."

Many students just rewrite f/g as f · g⁻¹ and use the product + chain rules instead. Both approaches give the same answer.

concepts.title: Polynomial Approximation
concepts.contentHtml:
Polynomials are easy to compute — just addition and multiplication. What if we could approximate any function using a polynomial?

That's exactly what a Taylor series does. Around a point a, we build a polynomial that matches the function's value, slope, curvature, and higher derivatives at that point.

The more terms we include, the better the approximation over a wider range.

concepts.title: Famous Taylor Series
concepts.contentHtml:
Some Taylor series are so important they're worth memorizing:

eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + … (converges everywhere!)

sin(x) = x - x³/3! + x⁵/5! - … (only odd powers)

cos(x) = 1 - x²/2! + x⁴/4! - … (only even powers)

1/(1-x) = 1 + x + x² + x³ + … (geometric series, |x| < 1)

concepts.title: Convergence & Euler's Identity
concepts.contentHtml:
A Taylor series may converge (give the correct value) only within a certain radius of convergence.

The geometric series 1/(1-x) only converges for |x| < 1. But eˣ, sin, and cos converge for all x.

The ultimate payoff: combining the series for eˣ, sin, and cos with imaginary numbers gives Euler's identity, often called the most beautiful equation in mathematics.

concepts.title: What is a Differential Equation?
concepts.contentHtml:
A differential equation (DE) is an equation that involves a function and its derivatives.

Instead of solving for a number, you solve for a function.

Example: dy/dx = 2x. What function has derivative 2x? Answer: y = x² + C.

DEs model everything from population growth to radioactive decay to the motion of planets.

concepts.title: Separation of Variables
concepts.contentHtml:
The simplest technique: if you can get all the y's on one side and all the x's on the other, you can integrate both sides separately.

Example: dy/dx = ky (exponential growth)

Separate: dy/y = k dx

Integrate: ln|y| = kx + C

Solve: y = Aeᵏˣ

This gives the exponential growth model — the solution to the simplest differential equation.

concepts.title: Second-Order & Oscillation
concepts.contentHtml:
A second-order DE involves the second derivative. The most famous one describes a spring:

y'' = -ω²y

"Acceleration is proportional to displacement but opposite in direction." The solution is sinusoidal oscillation: y = A cos(ωt) + B sin(ωt).

This single equation explains pendulums, vibrating strings, AC circuits, and even quantum wavefunctions.
mathExpressions: y'' + \omega^2 y = 0 \implies y = A\cos(\omega t) + B\sin(\omega t)

concepts.title: Partial Derivatives
concepts.contentHtml:
When a function has multiple inputs, like f(x, y) = x²y + 3y, we can take a derivative with respect to one variable while holding the others constant.

∂f/∂x treats y as a constant and differentiates with respect to x.

∂f/∂y treats x as a constant and differentiates with respect to y.

For f(x,y) = x²y + 3y: ∂f/∂x = 2xy, ∂f/∂y = x² + 3.

concepts.title: The Gradient
concepts.contentHtml:
The gradient collects all partial derivatives into a vector. It points in the direction of steepest ascent.

For f(x,y): ∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y)

This is the foundation of gradient descent in machine learning: to minimize a loss function, you move in the direction opposite to the gradient.

The gradient's magnitude tells you how steep the hill is.

concepts.title: Multiple Integrals & Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
Just as single integrals find area under curves, double integrals find volume under surfaces, and triple integrals find hypervolume.

The major theorems of multivariable calculus — Green's, Stokes', and the Divergence theorem — all generalize the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to higher dimensions.

They connect integrals over regions to integrals over their boundaries, and are essential in physics and engineering.
mathExpressions: \iint_R f(x,y)\, dA, \quad \oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_R \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) dA

title: Sequences & Series
description: Convergence, power series, and analytic functions

concepts.title: Convergence of Sequences
concepts.contentHtml:
A sequence (a_n) converges to a limit L if the terms get arbitrarily close to L as n grows. Formally, for every epsilon > 0, there exists N such that |a_n - L| < epsilon for all n > N.

A Cauchy sequence is one where the terms get arbitrarily close to each other: for every epsilon > 0, there exists N such that |a_m - a_n| < epsilon for all m, n > N.

In the real numbers, a sequence converges if and only if it is Cauchy. This is the completeness of the reals -- there are no "gaps" for sequences to fall into.
mathExpressions: a_n \to L \iff \forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists N : n > N \implies |a_n - L| < \varepsilon

concepts.title: Series Convergence Tests
concepts.contentHtml:
A series is the sum of a sequence: S = sum of a_n. It converges if the partial sums S_N = a_1 + a_2 + ... + a_N approach a finite limit.

Key tests for convergence:

Ratio test: If |a_{n+1}/a_n| approaches L < 1, the series converges absolutely. If L > 1, it diverges.

Root test: If |a_n|^{1/n} approaches L < 1, the series converges absolutely.

Comparison test: If 0 <= a_n <= b_n and the sum of b_n converges, so does the sum of a_n.

Integral test: If f(n) = a_n where f is positive and decreasing, then the sum and the integral from 1 to infinity of f converge or diverge together.

concepts.title: Power Series & Analytic Functions
concepts.contentHtml:
A power series is a series of the form sum of c_n (x - a)^n. It converges within some radius of convergence R around the center a.

Inside the radius, the series converges absolutely. Outside, it diverges. On the boundary |x - a| = R, anything can happen.

The radius can be found via the ratio or root test: R = 1 / lim |c_{n+1}/c_n| (when this limit exists).

A function that equals its power series in a neighborhood of every point in its domain is called analytic. Most familiar functions (polynomials, exp, sin, cos) are analytic. Analytic functions are infinitely differentiable and completely determined by their Taylor coefficients.

title: Vector Calculus
description: Fields, line integrals, and the great theorems

concepts.title: Vector Fields & Differential Operators
concepts.contentHtml:
A vector field assigns a vector to every point in space -- think of wind velocity at each location, or the gravitational pull at each point around a planet.

Three fundamental differential operators act on vector fields:

Gradient (grad f = nabla f): Takes a scalar field to a vector field pointing uphill.

Divergence (div F = nabla . F): Measures how much a vector field "spreads out" from a point. Positive divergence = source, negative = sink.

Curl (curl F = nabla x F): Measures the rotational tendency of a field. Nonzero curl means the field "swirls."
mathExpressions: \nabla f = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\right)
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial F_2}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial F_3}{\partial z}

concepts.title: Line & Surface Integrals
concepts.contentHtml:
A line integral integrates a function or vector field along a curve. For a vector field F along curve C, the line integral measures the total "work" done by F along C.

A surface integral integrates over a 2D surface in 3D space. For a vector field, the surface integral measures the total "flux" -- how much of the field passes through the surface.

These integrals are the building blocks of the three great theorems of vector calculus.

concepts.title: Green's, Stokes', and the Divergence Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Three theorems unify vector calculus by relating integrals over a region to integrals over its boundary:

Green's Theorem (2D): The circulation of F around a closed curve C equals the double integral of curl F over the enclosed region R. Example: to find the work done by a force around a loop, integrate the curl over the interior instead.

Stokes' Theorem (3D curves/surfaces): The line integral of F around the boundary of a surface S equals the surface integral of curl F over S.

Divergence Theorem (3D volumes): The flux of F through a closed surface S equals the triple integral of div F over the enclosed volume V. Example: the total outflow through a closed surface equals the total "source strength" inside.

All three are higher-dimensional versions of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: integral over interior = evaluation on boundary.

concepts.title: Complex Functions & Cauchy-Riemann
concepts.contentHtml:
A complex function f(z) maps complex numbers to complex numbers. Writing z = x + iy and f(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y), a function is holomorphic (complex-differentiable) if it satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations.

These two simple equations impose incredibly strong constraints: holomorphic functions are automatically infinitely differentiable, analytic (equal to their Taylor series), and satisfy the maximum principle.

Being holomorphic is far more restrictive than being real-differentiable. This rigidity is what gives complex analysis its power.
mathExpressions: \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}

concepts.title: Contour Integration & Cauchy's Formula
concepts.contentHtml:
Contour integration is integration along paths in the complex plane. The fundamental result is Cauchy's Integral Theorem: the integral of a holomorphic function around any closed loop is zero (if the interior is in the domain).

Cauchy's Integral Formula is even more remarkable: a holomorphic function's value at any point inside a contour is completely determined by its values on the contour:

This means knowing a holomorphic function on a circle tells you everything about it inside. No real-valued analog exists!

concepts.title: Residue Theorem & Applications
concepts.contentHtml:
When a function has singularities (poles) inside a contour, the integral is no longer zero. Instead, it equals 2 pi i times the sum of residues at each pole.

A residue is the coefficient of the 1/(z - z_0) term in the Laurent series expansion around a singularity.

The real magic: the residue theorem can evaluate real integrals that are otherwise extremely difficult. By cleverly choosing contours in the complex plane, integrals like the integral from -infinity to infinity of sin(x)/x dx = pi fall out effortlessly.

title: Measure Theory & Lebesgue Integration
description: A more powerful theory of integration

concepts.title: Why Riemann Integration Isn't Enough
concepts.contentHtml:
The Dirichlet function equals 1 on rationals and 0 on irrationals. It's not Riemann integrable because every interval contains both rationals and irrationals, so upper and lower Riemann sums never agree.

Yet intuitively, the rationals are "negligible" (they form a countable set in an uncountable real line), so the integral "should" be 0.

Riemann integration also has problems with limits: the limit of a sequence of Riemann-integrable functions may not be Riemann-integrable, and you can't always interchange limits and integrals. These failures motivated a better theory.

concepts.title: Sigma-Algebras & Measures
concepts.contentHtml:
A sigma-algebra on a set X is a collection of subsets closed under complements and countable unions. It tells us which sets are "measurable."

A measure assigns a non-negative size to each measurable set, generalizing the notion of length/area/volume. The most important example is Lebesgue measure on the real line, which assigns the interval [a,b] the measure b - a.

A measurable function is one where preimages of measurable sets are measurable. This is the class of functions we can integrate in the Lebesgue sense.

Key insight: single points (and even countable sets like the rationals) have Lebesgue measure zero. Sets of measure zero are "negligible" for integration.

concepts.title: Lebesgue Integral & Convergence Theorems
concepts.contentHtml:
The Lebesgue integral partitions the range of a function (instead of the domain, as Riemann does). For each value y, measure the set where f(x) is approximately y, and sum up y times that measure.

This approach handles the Dirichlet function easily: the set where f = 1 (the rationals) has measure 0, so the integral is 0, as expected.

The greatest payoff is the Dominated Convergence Theorem: if f_n converges to f pointwise, and all f_n are bounded by an integrable function g, then the integral of f_n converges to the integral of f. You can freely interchange limits and integrals under a simple boundedness condition.

This theorem is the workhorse of modern analysis, probability theory, and functional analysis.
mathExpressions: f_n \to f \text{ pointwise}, \; |f_n| \le g \implies \int f_n \to \int f
